canonical_definition: Across the surveyed literature, the most prevalent framing of data efficiency is a model's ability to achieve strong performance with limited training data. This is broadly defined as either requiring a smaller absolute amount of data to reach a performance target or learning effectively from few examples, demonstrations, or feedback. While this core idea is consistent, its specific manifestation varies by context; for instance, in policy learning it is described as improving from few demonstrations, while in generative or embodied settings it can refer to minimizing oracle calls, candidate solutions, or environmental interactions. The construct is operationalized and measured through model performance in data-scarce scenarios on benchmarks including ALFWorld, VirtualHome, GrailQA, and FGVC. Data efficiency is also studied in relation to Reward Modeling. Several papers propose mechanisms that are reported to improve data efficiency, including a model's capacity for Relational reasoning, Self-reflection, and Task decomposition. Other reported drivers are algorithmic, such as In-context reinforcement learning and Attention sparsity, with one study noting that sparsity is a "key factor of the improvement induced by CoT" ("From Sparse Dependence to Sparse Attention..."). The ability to leverage pre-trained knowledge is also frequently cited as a source of data efficiency, as noted in papers like "Vision-Language Foundation Models as Effective Robot Imitators".
